etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English puple, peple, peeple, from Anglo-Norman people, from Old French pueple, peuple, pople, from Latin populus (“a people, nation”), from Old Latin populus, from earlier poplus, from even earlier poplos, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”) of unknown origin. Doublet of pueblo. Gradually ousted native English lede and, partially, folk.

Originally used with singular verbs (e.g. "the people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness" in the King James Version of 2 Samuel 17:29), the plural aspect of people is probably due to influence from Middle English lede, leed, a plural since Old English times; see lēode.

definitions.definition: plural of person: a body of persons considered generally or collectively; a group of two or more persons.

quote.citation: c. 1607, plaque recording the Bristol Channel floods:
quote.text: XXII people was in this parrish drownd.

quote.citation: 1813, Jane Austen, chapter 6, in Pride and Prejudice‎[1], →OCLC:
quote.text: "What a charming amusement for young people this is, Mr. Darcy! There is nothing like dancing after all. I consider it as one of the first refinements of polished society."

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: There were many wooden chairs for the bulk of his visitors, and two wicker armchairs with red cloth cushions for superior people. From the packing-cases had emerged some Indian clubs, […], and all these articles […] made a scattered and untidy decoration that Mrs. Clough assiduously dusted and greatly cherished.

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 1, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: “ […]  the awfully hearty sort of Christmas cards that people do send to other people that they don't know at all well. You know. The kind that have mottoes like  Here's rattling good luck and roaring good cheer, / With lashings of food and great hogsheads of beer. […]”

quote.citation: 2013 June 1, “Towards the end of poverty”, in The Economist‎[2], volume 407, number 8838, archived from the original on 23 October 2018, page 11:
quote.text: But poverty’s scourge is fiercest below $1.25 (the average of the 15 poorest countries’ own poverty lines, measured in 2005 dollars and adjusted for differences in purchasing power): people below that level live lives that are poor, nasty, brutish and short.

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Oliver Burkeman, “Conscious computing: how to take control of your life online”, in The Guardian Weekly‎[3], volume 189, number 2, archived from the original on August 24, 2013, page 27:
quote.text: The dirty secret of the internet is that all this distraction and interruption is immensely profitable. Web companies like to boast about […], or offering services that let you […] "share the things you love with the world" and so on. But the real way to build a successful online business is to be better than your rivals at undermining people's control of their own attention.

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “A punch in the gut”, in The Economist‎[4], volume 407, number 8842, archived from the original on 3 November 2018, pages 72–3:
quote.text: Mostly, the microbiome is beneficial. It helps with digestion and enables people to extract a lot more calories from their food than would otherwise be possible. Research over the past few years, however, has implicated it in diseases from atherosclerosis to asthma to autism.

definitions.definition: (countable, collective) Persons forming or belonging to a particular group, such as a nation, class, ethnic group, country, family, etc.

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: `So, oh Holly. This people was an old people before the Egyptians were.'

definitions.definition: A group of persons regarded as being servants, followers, companions or subjects of a ruler or leader.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Samuel 8:15, column 1:
quote.text: And Dauid reigned ouer all Iſrael, and Dauid executed iudgement and iuſtice vnto all his people.

quote.citation: 1952, Old Testament, Revised Standard Version, Thomas Nelson & Sons, Isaiah 1:3:
quote.text: The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's crib; but Israel does not know, my people does not understand.

quote.citation: 2001, Vince Flynn, Transfer of Power (fiction), Simon & Schuster, →ISBN, page 250:
quote.text: Kennedy looked down at Flood's desk and thought about the possibilities. "Can you locate him?""I already have my people checking on all three. So far I've only been able to confirm the whereabouts of the Jordanian officer."
Can I have one of my people get back to your people, Mr. President?" She tried to slam the phone back into the base and failed.

definitions.definition: A person's ancestors, relatives or family.
The mass of a community as distinguished from a special class (elite); the commonalty; the populace; the vulgar; the common crowd; the citizens.

quote.text: The people have spoken, the bastards.

definitions.definition: People in general, humans, by extension sentient beings real or fictional.
(transitive) To stock with people or inhabitants; to fill as with people; to populate.

quote.citation: 1674, John Dryden, The State of Innocence and the Fall of Man‎[5], act II, scene I:
quote.text: He would not be alone, who all things can; / But peopled Heav'n with Angels, Earth with Man.

quote.citation: 1837, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XXI, in Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides. […], volume II, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, page 159:
quote.text: Scenes, long since forgotten, had been peopling his solitude with one still cherished image paramount over all; one young fair face, whose sweet eyes seemed to look upon him reproachfully:...

definitions.definition: (transitive) To inhabit; to occupy; to populate.

quote.citation: a. 1645, John Milton, Il Penseroso, lines 7–8:
quote.text: […]  / As thick and numberless / As the gay motes that people the Sun Beams, /  […]

definitions.definition: (rare, informal) To interact with people; to socialize.

quote.citation: 2018, Jennifer L. Armentrout, The Darkest Star, Tor Teen, →ISBN, page 149:
quote.text: I don't people well.” “Not peopling well is a crap excuse,” I retorted, and started to step around him, but a sudden thought occurred to me.
My head tilted as Calvin said, "Don't worry about him. He just doesn't people well.The fuck? I people. Sometimes. With people I know.

quote.citation: 2020, Teri Anne Stanley, Lucky Chance Cowboy, Sourcebooks, Inc., →ISBN:
quote.text: I don't people well.” He laughed at that. “You do okay,” he assured her.
